catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic in Alto Perené. ... Syllable weight, ranked from the highest to the lowest CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV > V, tends to determine stress assignment in independent words ... As seen in (2.34), syllables with branching nuclei (a long vowel or a diphthong), and/or a coda (C)VV, CVN, (C)VVN) are likely to attract stress. But there are also exceptions, e.g., shin.'ki 'maize'. ... Based on the sonority scale of Alto Perené vowels, arranged from the strongest to the weakest, a > o, e > i, the stress in (2.35) is assigned to the syllable ... penultimate syllable, as seen in (2.36). new_statements.quote: La acentuación de «jaká» (y de los otros deícticos adverbiales de lugar derivados de la protoestructura <ja>) contraviene las reglas de acentuación en asháninka, donde generalmente estas son graves. Sin embargo, existe una tendencia de la dependencia de la acentuación de la sonoridad del núcleo silábico, por lo que se considera que la escala de sonoridad de las vocales en asháninka es la siguiente: [a] > [e] > [o] > [i]. Además, se considera fonémico por lo que permite diferenciar significados. Además, el alargamiento puede ser usado como una estrategia discursiva para enfatizar la naturaleza del evento (Mihas, 2010: 50, 75).
new_statements.translation: The stress of «jaká» (and of the other adverbial place deictics derived from the proto-structure <ja>) goes against the stress rules of Asháninka, where [words] are generally paroxytone [stressed on the penultimate syllable]. However, there is a tendency for stress to depend on the sonority of the syllabic nucleus, so the vowel sonority scale of Asháninka is taken to be [a] > [e] > [o] > [i]. Moreover, it [vowel length] is considered phonemic since it distinguishes meanings; and lengthening can be used as a discourse strategy to emphasize the nature of the event (Mihas 2010: 50, 75).

new_statements.rule_in_words: As reported second-hand: stress in Alto Perené Ashéninka is generally on the penultimate syllable, with a tendency for stress to be attracted by more sonorous nuclei (a > e > o > i); the final-stressed place deictics jaká, jará, jantá, jantó are exceptions. The primary description (Mihas 2015: 56-58; Mihas 2010: 50, 75) was not seen; Pedrós 2023: 81 states that Mihas' Alto Perené patterns are 'quite different' from the Ucayali-Pajonal ones 'above all in disyllabic words', so the penultimate default should be treated as unverified. Related Kampan varieties (Pichis, Apurucayali, Ucayali-Pajonal, Nanti) are described as weight-/quality-sensitive iambic systems with final extrametricality, so a weight-sensitive reading is plausible for the primary source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Alto Perené. (Pedrós 2023 §2.5 reports secondary stresses on enclitics and in longer words for Ucayali-Pajonal only.)
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed place deictics jaká/jará/jantá/jantó (Solari 2020: 112); a vowel-sonority tendency a > e > o > i overriding the default.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark about isolated deictic adverbs in a syntax/semantics thesis; no citation-form vs phrase discussion. Vowel length is separately noted as phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Solari 2020) calls the variety 'asháninka del Alto Perené' (data from Perené-valley communities, Chanchamayo, Junín) — this is the Alto/Upper Perené variety described by Mihas, i.e. ashe1272 (ISO prq), not Tambo-Ene Asháninka (cni). Pedrós 2023 (LOT 640), the only open grammar with a full stress section, describes Ucayali-Pajonal Ashéninka (Gran Pajonal/Ucayali; ISO cjo/cpb group), a different Glottolog languoid; its §2.5 must not be read as an ashe1272 description — it only points to Mihas 2015: 56-58 for Alto Perené and says the Alto Perené patterns differ from its own.

new_statements.quote: Los cuatro tipos de sílabas encajan en un patrón de acentuación alterna que hace que el acento sea predecible en el ashéninca. [...] el patrón de acentuación empieza en la segunda sílaba y se acentúan todas las sílabas pares a la derecha, pero no la última sílaba de la palabra [p. 36] [...] Todas las sílabas fuertes son acentuadas, salvo cuando están al final de la palabra [p. 37] [...] El acento primario recae sobre la última sílaba fuerte que puede ser la penúltima, la antepenúltima y la antes de la antepenúltima sílaba. [...] Si ninguna de las cuatro últimas sílabas es fuerte, el acento primario recae en la última sílaba que lleva acento. [p. 42]
new_statements.translation: The four syllable types fit into an alternating stress pattern that makes stress predictable in Ashéninca. [...] the stress pattern begins on the second syllable and all even-numbered syllables to the right are stressed, but not the last syllable of the word [p. 36] [...] All strong syllables are stressed, except when they are at the end of the word [p. 37] [...] Primary stress falls on the last strong syllable, which may be the penultimate, the antepenultimate or the pre-antepenultimate syllable. [...] If none of the last four syllables is strong, primary stress falls on the last syllable that carries stress. [p. 42]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Syllables are ranked strong (long vowel or diphthong) > normal (a, o, e, or i closed by a nasal) > weak (open i) > dead (shi, tsi). Default pattern: stress on the 2nd syllable and every even syllable thereafter, never on the final syllable. Strong syllables are always stressed (except word-finally) and restart the alternating count. Disyllables stress the first syllable, except dead + voiceless-onset second syllable (tsi.CA 'where'), which stress the second. Weak syllables take pattern stress only under conditions of word length and speech rate; dead syllables never take it (stress shifts to an adjacent syllable). Primary stress = the last strong syllable if it is among the last four syllables; otherwise the last stressed syllable (in all-normal words the penult); exception: if the last stressed syllable is weak and the preceding stressed one is normal, the normal one takes primary stress (p. 43).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: words carry multiple stresses; all non-primary stresses (alternating even syllables from the left, and strong syllables) are secondary; 'Después del acento primario, no hay acento secundario' (p. 42).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables with dead first syllable + voiceless-onset second syllable stress the final syllable (tsi.CA, shi.THA); weak syllables lose/keep pattern stress depending on word length (3-, 4-, 5+-syllable words) and slow vs rapid speech (pp. 38-40); dead syllables shift stress to an adjacent syllable (pp. 40-42); normal syllable before a strong one may optionally lose stress (p. 38); primary-stress exception with weak final stressed syllable (p. 43).
new_statements.identity_note: Neither listed work is a description of Alto Perené proper. Payne 1989 (SLP 28) covers Ashéninka of the Pichis primarily, with Alto Perené (PE) variants in brackets and in the stress review (its p. 14: 'trata principalmente de la variedad ashéninca del Pichis.. Asimismo se incluyen notas sobre la variedad del Alto Perené'); SIL's record lists both cpu and prq as subject languages, Glottolog files it under cpu. Payne, Payne & Sánchez 1982 (SLP 18) is explicitly Ashéninca del Apurucayali [cpc]. Both listed open_urls (old sil.org/americas/peru show_work.asp links) are dead; the current records are https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/29992 and /29935, whose PDFs are an automated-access block-challenged by automated download, so both copies were taken from Internet Archive copy of the SIL files (2024-07-25 and 2024-07-10). Both PDFs are scans without a text layer; the stress pages were scanned (tesseract spa+eng, 200 dpi), so quotes are scanned text checked by eye against the page images' sense.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction on type: both Payne works and the existing Solari 2020 statement (and the Google Books fragments of Mihas 2015 already held by the project) describe a non-phonemic, weight-sensitive system with alternating secondary stresses and a penultimate default in words without heavy syllables. One detail differs between the Payne (Pichis/Apurucayali) descriptions and the Mihas 2015 Alto Perené fragments held by the project: Payne 1989 says strong syllables are NOT stressed word-finally (p. 37) and Payne et al. 1982 say a phrase-final strong syllable shifts stress to the penult (p. 187-188), whereas the Mihas 2015 snippet says 'primary stress is assigned to the ultimate syllable, if it is heavy, and otherwise, to the penultimate syllable'. Pedrós 2023: 81 (held by the project) also notes Mihas's Alto Perené patterns differ from his Ucayali-Pajonal ones 'above all in disyllabic words'. Payne 1989 stresses the first syllable of ordinary disyllables (sá.ri, shí.ma) but the second in tsi./shi.-initial disyllables with a voiceless onset (tsi.cá, shi.thá).

sources.note: Describes UCAYALI-PAJONAL Ashéninka (not ashe1272): stress non-phonemic, tendency-based; di-/trisyllables penult, tetrasyllables antepenult, bimoraic syllables strongest attractors, iambic feet in longer words. On p. 81 it says: 'Payne, Payne & Sánchez (1982:185-95) describe the stress patterns for Apurucayali and Mihas (2015a:56-58) for Alto Perené.. Regarding Mihas' patterns, they are quite different from mine, above all in disyllabic words.' So the Alto Perené stress description is Mihas 2015: 56-58; content not given.
